title: The scholar's mistake
hookLine: a person can recite the driving manual and still run the red light: the Patti says reading without living the letters is still not learning

lines: THE MANUAL, AND THE RED LIGHT.
cards: A driving test comes in two parts. One happens at a desk, with a pencil. The other happens at a real crossing, with a real car coming.

Someone can pass the first and fail the second, and only the second keeps anyone safe on the road. The Patti has a sharp line about which one counts, in the second half of its center line, the half we held back yesterday.

teach.b: Yesterday the Rahao spoke to the mind: why do you forget, foolish mind? Here's how it finishes, in paraphrase: when you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted as educated.
The word for educated is parhiaa: one who has read. So the Patti redefines a reader. You haven't really read until you can give an account of your life.
Not of the book. Of your life. That's the scholar's mistake: thinking the reading is the finish line.
Second, the letter ngangai says it straight out.
In paraphrase: whoever understands true wisdom, that one is the learned pandit. And the next line shows what that looks like: one who knows the One in all beings doesn't go around saying I, I.
The proof of learning isn't how much you can recite. It's whether you see the One in the person in front of you, and let go of your own self-importance.
Third, this isn't a poem against study. Guru Nanak put deep teaching on a schoolboard; the Patti honors the letters. It just won't let them stay on the board.
Fourth, think about the account the Rahao means. Not a test score. A life story with the deeds left in.
Did dadai make you blame less?
Did tatai make you put on less of a show? Did sasai make you see one Master over everyone? That's the exam.
A person who has never read a word could pass it. A person who has read everything could fail.

how: Sikh teaching pairs study of Gurbani with living it, often summed up as reading the Guru's word and then practicing it in daily conduct, seva and honest work.

o: trusting a teacher instead of the book
thinking reading is the finish line
misspelling a word in the holy text

games.q: the scholar's mistake — tap the pairs.
p: one who has read: the educated one
when you give it, you're counted educated
who understands wisdom is the pandit
the one who knows the One

s: the Patti says study is a waste of time
it honors the letters and puts deep teaching on a schoolboard; it just won't let them stay there.
the Rahao says you're counted educated when you give your account
when you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted as educated.

games.q: you've read every book on the shelf. by the Patti's measure, are you educated yet?
o: only when you can give the account of your life.
games.why: the Rahao says it: when you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted as educated.

practice: Pick one word from the Patti's letters, made, from sasai, blame no one, from dadai, or no show, from tatai, and think of one real moment in the hours ahead where it could show up: a meeting, a phone call, a line at the store.
See yourself there, living the word instead of just knowing it, then let the picture go and rest with the breath. If you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: The scholar's mistake. Thinking reading is the finish line. The Patti says you're counted educated when you can give the account of your life, and the pandit is the one who sees the One in all. Today's word.

orig.note: parhiaa: one who has read, the educated one; the Patti says you are this when you give your account.

carryVoice: Your line: live the letters. The real exam is a life. Talk soon.
